trail: Core thesis: how public capacity turns into private infrastructure, then power
question: Did post-Cold War governments hand strategy, expertise, risk and delivery to private and hybrid firms in a way that let some actors shape the choices on offer, keep control, and become hard to remove or replace?
found: Nothing by itself: it is a written framework of five overlapping eras (1991 to today) and seven steps (who framed the problem, who chose the options, which document made it official, who got control, when it became unavoidable, who kept the value, could the public undo it). It forbids itself from asserting any finding; the real testing happened in the stress-test trail.
risk: The framing text says some founder-led tech/defense networks 'appear to have pursued' the gap deliberately after 2011; the later stress test did not support that as a system-wide claim.
why: The organizing idea everything else hangs on; cheap to keep.

trail: Stress test of the core thesis (Palantir, Anduril, ICE, Army, Ukraine, Erebor bank)
question: When the thesis is attacked head-on, which parts survive against real public records (GAO audits, court rulings, SEC filings, Army and ICE documents, Ukrainian Ministry of Defence)?
found: Seven rounds produced 63 narrow rulings (an eighth, on the Erebor bank and its investors, followed): 42 supported for human review, 8 need more records, 5 turned out to be non-links, 8 stay unproven, none disproved. Supported: DoD cut its buying staff in the 1990s then leaned on contractors (GAO: at least $33.9B over ~57,000 Iraq/Afghanistan contracts), a court ruled the Army skipped required commercial-item steps in a Palantir dispute, Palantir's founders keep voting control and government is 54% of its revenue, and Palantir and Anduril work together in the Army's NGC2 program. Not supported: one founder-controlled network running it all, 'hidden' Palantir control (SEC filings disclose it), a direct Palantir-to-ICE risk-scoring link, and personal enrichment; the revised thesis explicitly keeps competition and public institutions as real forces.
risk: Centered on Palantir/Anduril; all rulings made by the project's own maintainers with AI help, no independent reviewer; 'supported for human review' is not 'proven'.
why: The one place the big theory was actually tested against real documents, with honest non-links.

trail: Mapping every known research object onto the thesis (plus the Ukraine-war phase)
question: Can each of the roughly 690 cases, source routes, reports and open questions across 24 sectors be assigned to a thesis era and step, and does the 2022+ Ukraine war form its own phase?
found: Bookkeeping result only: 690 known items across 24 sectors; at the last count 59 were mapped by hand, 489 known-but-unmapped, 142 unresolved. The Ukraine lens (four sub-phases from emergency improvisation in 2022 to permanent readiness 2026+) is defined but concludes nothing; its only evidence is the separate stress-test round on Ukraine's Brave1 combat-data platform.
risk: Progress is measured in rows labelled, not in anything learned; most rows are still unmapped.
why: A coverage checklist, but low payoff for the effort.

trail: Synthetic populations: are AI-modelled publics becoming decision infrastructure?
question: Do public records show 'synthetic population' systems (AI stand-ins for real people or audiences) becoming a layer used by governments and companies, moving through people, official legitimacy, deployment, technology and money, and when do modelled publics replace observed ones?
found: Six sub-claims and 16 planned case studies are laid out, but only 2 cases have real extracts (11 UK government documents). They show a former No. 10 health adviser's paid consultancy came with official conditions and, separately, a 2026 rules breach on other work, alongside official statements that nothing suggested a reward; and that No. 10 Data Science, i.AI and GDS were separate units that collaborated and were later merged in other combinations, with no source saying 10DS became i.AI. The Gartner vendor list is blocked (licensed report not obtained, 14 vendor names recovered from public posts); zero evidence has been formally accepted.
risk: Names a private-sector consultant (former official) in a one-person case; also includes a prepared-but-unsent legal request to a private UK company (Electric Twin) for its shareholder register.
why: A fresh non-defense, real-world question with clean sourcing, but only 2 of 16 cases started.

trail: Epistemic ceiling (K0) part 1: do the owner's ten named cases hold up?
question: When a powerful person can't recognize an expert's competence, do they relabel the expert as the problem and use their power over jobs, publication or access to remove the person who could have corrected them? Do ten hand-picked public figures fit?
found: Thirteen events involving ten public figures were source-checked. Six are well documented step by step (Musk firing a Twitter engineer who corrected him and the later ranking change, the LA Times endorsement veto, the Washington Post opinion-section change, New College of Florida tenure denials and the state's follow-up); seven are not established, with the documented chain falling to zero for the RFK Jr. vaccine-panel removal and both Hegseth removals and to one step for Zuckerberg's cutoff of NYU ad researchers. None disproved; 23 of 25 source pages retrieved but none saved byte-for-byte, and the checking was done by the maintainers with AI help.
risk: The published report page names living people (Musk, Bezos, Hegseth, RFK Jr., Zuckerberg, Rufo, DeSantis, Dean, Soon-Shiong) next to 'dismissal/veto/removal' labels; the list came from the owner's own essay; no independent review; the mechanism reads like a psychological claim.
why: Strong idea and honest downgrades, but the named-person version needs independent review before staying public.

trail: Epistemic ceiling (K0) part 2: neutral search for the same pattern
question: If you search official oversight records without starting from famous names, how often does 'expert contradicts boss, expert reclassified as the problem, expert removed, institution loses its error detector' actually appear?
found: Eight rounds, nine fixed search templates and about 300 hits kept 65 records, of which about 28 were close calls; in the seven rounds checked, 8 were rated worth human review, the strongest reaching 6 of 7 steps: the Challenger launch decision and engineer, East River helicopter pilot warnings, the SickKids/Apotex drug-trial dispute, and an INS official who testified to Congress. Zero cases were formally admitted because no independent reviewer has signed off, and the control cases show appeals, stays and regulators often did work, so the pattern is real in famous safety cases but not shown to be general.
risk: Zero independent reviews; the final round is not yet checked; strongest hits are decades-old non-political cases, so they say little about today's politics.
why: Best-run piece of the theory work: neutral search, controls, honest negatives.

trail: Counter-selector 1: finding people whose real output beats their title
question: Can you systematically recognize people or small teams who repeatedly produce valid results despite low status or resources, without just picking people who resemble someone?
found: Built a 30-case test set in six classes (including deliberate false positives and high-status controls), mostly drawn from the whistleblower cases above; 18 had enough public material for two blind reviews each. Result: zero 'complete' people found, three near-misses (clinical-trial researcher Olivieri, Elliot Richardson, fired U.S. attorney David Iglesias), and Richardson reached 7 of 8 capability tests but failed the 'output beyond resources' test against all four comparison lanes. Three real emails were sent on 1 Aug to the Library of Congress, UN Archives and Carter Library asking for papers (no useful reply; the UN auto-refused), and a public GitHub review request drew zero responses.
risk: Scores named real people (some living) and prepares 'field tests' and contact; an agent sent emails from the owner's account; the framing is close to the 'status allocator' it criticizes.
why: Interesting question, but 25 rounds produced no person finding.

trail: Counter-selector 2: test it on living open-source and public-service maintainers
question: After the archive route stalled, can the same test work on people whose work is publicly traceable today (maintainers of security tools, data tools, breach-notification services)?
found: Four lanes were reviewed blind: eight bounded person-level supports in total (exception handling, openness to correction, restraint) plus several at team or service level. No lane shows a verified successor or handoff, so the count of complete people stays zero and no contact or ranking was authorized.
risk: Assesses named living people (Stenberg, Willison, Troy Hunt) who don't know about it.
why: Better data than archives, but still no person-level result.

trail: Counter-selector 3: can a project's working state really be handed to a successor?
question: Does any public project show a complete, acknowledged handoff (authority, credentials, dependencies, open decisions, rollback, successor actually running)?
found: Ten rounds found only partial examples (PyTorch lead-maintainer change, Aave risk-service rotation, Debian leader handovers, a live process swap in E2B, a saved-container restore in CRI-O) and one small package the project built itself that survives a corrupted-copy test. Zero examples with every required part, and only one person (Daniel Stenberg) gained a new bounded support.
risk: Drifted into low-level software engineering (container checkpointing) far from the original question; 205 automated self-tests of its own rules.
why: Detour away from people and the real world.

trail: Distributed counterpower aversion: do actors with different motives still protect the powerful from binding correction?
question: Can separate actors with different ideologies and goals repeatedly act in ways that keep a protected center free from outside correction, without any central plan?
found: Nothing yet: it is a hypothesis with five candidate mechanisms (status signalling, personnel moving between roles, compatible systems, selection effects, alternatives closed off), twelve search categories and twelve frozen queries, but none has been run. It bans any conclusion about coordination, shared purpose, motive or personal hostility.
risk: Partly personal in origin (it rules out concluding that any group is collectively shunning a person); easy to over-read; the page on the site shows only the scaffold.
why: Runs on K0's search; worth running before building more around it.

trail: Who holds the rule-making seat, who just operates, and who knows it (constitutional class and awareness)
question: Inside these systems, who is the sovereign, host, operator, gatekeeper, worker or acted-upon person, how much of the system do they demonstrably understand, and what power do they have to change it?
found: Sorted 31 real parties (Palantir founders and staff, the Army program office, NHS England, ICE users, Brave1, Google and Microsoft worker coalitions, courts, venture firms) on five axes using 27 public sources; 14 of 18 categories have an example. Main finding is a gap: of three 'acted-upon' records, none speaks in their own voice, and the operator/gatekeeper middle layer is by far the largest group.
risk: Gives named people and firms 'awareness' ratings, i.e. judgments about what they know; small sample.
why: Useful for spotting missing voices; rating individuals is shaky.

trail: Who may act on a hunch and who must prove injury afterward (epistemic jurisdiction)
question: Who is allowed to turn uncertainty into action, who sets the threshold, and who has to prove harm after the fact once a system is deployed?
found: Fifteen systems (Palantir/Army/ICE/NHS/Brave1 plus comparators Post Office Horizon, Wisconsin COMPAS, Idaho Medicaid tool, Dutch SyRI, Australian Robodebt, ICE student-visa terminations) were run through eight tests: 122 records, 66 sources, 76 supported for human review, 29 need more records, 14 unproven, 3 non-links. The burden-of-proof asymmetry is firmest where courts or inquiries forced the record (Horizon, Robodebt); a single cross-system pattern is not promoted.
risk: Outside my assigned list, so it may overlap other slices; same maintainer-only review caveat.
why: Most transferable idea in the pile; works on well-documented scandals.

trail: Continuous source monitoring (evidence hydrology, global circulation, source ecology v2)
question: Can a scheduled, automatic watch over a few hundred official, court, direct-voice and archive sources across 12 world regions keep the research fed without bypassing access limits or treating web reachability as evidence?
found: Defined 128 sources/18 catchments (hydrology) then 192 sources/12 regional basins/96 polls (circulation). The one real run recorded: 63 of 96 routes reachable (66%), 60 gave usable content, 33 failed (20 blocked, 7 rate-limited), 9 of 12 basins healthy; a second-version repair plan was written but never observed live, and no conclusion about the world came out of it.
risk: Scheduled to run unattended (four times a day on GitHub) against many third-party sites; measures whether websites respond, not what they say.
why: Plumbing, not research; keep only if you want automatic freshness checks.

trail: POOF and Clifford: turning a private manuscript into a public, challengeable publication system
question: How can the evidence database be paired with a narrative publication (a manuscript, reader file, expert examination and archive) so that facts flow out, challenges flow back in, and the narrative never writes new facts?
found: Nothing about the world: it is a design with a one-way rule, four reader-facing layers, five transaction types, two new report types (an 'epistemic ceiling dossier' codenamed REAL STEEL and a 'two-tier rules audit' called Steel Mirror), and a generated review site with machine-readable endpoints. The private manuscript is not in the repo, nothing is deployed, and no outside review exists.
risk: Depends on a private book that isn't in the repo; builds API/agent interfaces for a site that doesn't exist; not on the public site (kept private).
why: Only matters if the book/publication is real; otherwise premature.

trail: Project stable ground: twelve checkpoints of 'what is actually established'
question: At any moment, what is established fact, what is hypothesis, and what exists only in an unmerged branch, and what must future work not break?
found: Twelve numbered checkpoints in four days (29 Jul to 1 Aug) freeze the state of the project; the standing numbers are blunt: zero external reproductions, zero outside adoption, zero independent reviewers, 'works standard' not met, project not complete. Also records a rule never to wait for outside reviewers or ask the owner to recruit strangers.
risk: Pure internal process; each checkpoint is about the repo's own state.
why: Candid status ledger, but most useful as a single page, not twelve.

trail: Allocator war: does anti-DEI policy end selection or move who does the selecting?
question: Is the current fight over who defines merit, eligibility and admissible evidence, and who keeps the power to correct, a transfer of selection power rather than its removal, and does it link to defense-capital programs?
found: From 15 public sources, 14 observations: 5 show selection power being moved to new selectors, 1 shows public programs converting into selected private capacity, 2 are effective independent counterweights, 2 are ordinary industrial-policy controls, 3 are open questions, 1 stronger inference was refused. Narrow conclusion only: no support for a racial-order, prevalence, coordination or common-purpose claim, and no independent review yet.
risk: Grew from a politically charged essay (a 'status-for-sovereignty compact' about the MAGA coalition) while the project's own rule says no lane may start because an actor is disliked or politically convenient; kept off the rendered site for now.
why: Careful narrow result, but needs independent review before it is anything.

trail: Are the project's search universes fair? (selection-neutrality reviews)
question: For each topic area the project chose to investigate, was the set of people and institutions searched defined neutrally, or gerrymandered toward a target?
found: Eight search universes are logged (AI policy, defense NatSec100, official records, LinkedIn private attention, Epstein public corpus, Trump-office business capital, Panama offshore providers, K0 ceiling events): zero cleared, seven waiting for an independent challenger, one not applicable. One lane (Trump-office business capital) already had to be rebuilt after failing two internal attacks for starting from the target.
risk: Without any independent reviewer every lane stays 'pending' forever; internal process.
why: Guards against the most obvious criticism of the whole project.

trail: Can outsiders understand and contribute? (comprehension test and contribution inbox)
question: Can a stranger, shown only the public material, correctly explain one result, and can an outsider safely submit a candidate link?
found: Nothing yet: one test route (a 112-person roster treated as background, not as links), four fixtures and a validator that by design can never say 'pass'; no human has taken the test. The contribution inbox holds only a README and a blank template, so zero outside contributions.
risk: Not linked from the public home page by design.
why: No readers or contributors, so no signal.

trail: Public reporter briefs (Anduril; Arcadia, California)
question: Can the case records be turned into a readable briefing that shows the public-record sequence without alleging wrongdoing?
found: Two briefings are live. Anduril: 24 claims (15 verified, 9 need review), 21 public sources, 18 dated events, with counterexamples such as the GAO denying Anduril's 2021 protest and a competitively bid $642M Marine Corps contract with ten offers. Arcadia: 45 claims, 91 public links, a timeline from 1968 redevelopment to station-area approvals, framed against the ordinary 'growth machine' explanation; neither states a causal or wrongdoing conclusion.
risk: Both labelled 'review required' with no independent reviewer; Arcadia started from a chat conversation. Overlaps the case-specific slices.
why: The only reader-facing output so far.

trail: Build instructions: the rules and the plan through 2037
question: What must the tool never do, and what stages (foundation 2026, second case 2026-27, signed releases 2027-29, federation 2029-32, succession 2032-37) get it to a state a stranger could verify and extend?
found: A governing document with 11 never-change rules (a source for every link, shared places not 'knowing each other', no ethnicity-based aggregation, neutral selection) and a phased plan. Only Phase 0 is done (closed 8 Sep 2026: stable IDs, a cap on large rosters, narrated routes, source-quality upgrades, archived receipts); Phases 1 to 4 not started, e.g. the US defense case folder it calls for does not exist.
risk: A 2037 plan resting on one maintainer; it asks for three maintainers at separate institutions, signed releases and an agent query service that are far off.
why: Short statement of purpose and rules; the rest is aspirational.
